o: Repeatedly take the leftmost adjacent equal pair and replace it with their sum, until no adjacent equals remain. [3,1,1,2] becomes [3,2,2] then [3,4]. [2,2,4] becomes [4,4] then [8]. A fresh sum can equal its left neighbor, so merges cascade leftward, which is exactly what a stack models.
k: Process left to right with a stack: after pushing x, merge while the top two are equal (pop both, push double).
The leftmost-pair rule is automatically respected because any cascade triggered by a merge happens at the merge site before we ever look further right.

a.i: When we push x onto the stack, the only possible new adjacent-equal pair involves x and the previous top (everything below was already conflict-free). Merging doubles the top; the doubled value may itself equal the new top, hence the while loop. This reproduces the leftmost-first order exactly.
s: While the top two stack elements are equal, pop one and double the other.
a.t: O(n) amortized — each element is pushed once and merged at most log(sum) times overall

w: The stack is the natural interview answer; a naive list-rebuild simulation is O(n^2) and may TLE at n=1e5. Watch overflow in fixed-width languages: repeated doubling can reach about 2^30 * 1e5, exceeding 32-bit ints, so use 64-bit (the final values still fit in 64 bits). Edge cases: single element, all-equal arrays collapsing to one element.
